title: The Case That Limits Parliament

endcard.line: Pictures: Constitution of India (public domain); Sansad Bhavan (public domain); Subhashish Panigrahi, Pinakpani (CC BY-SA 4.0)

segments.say: Can Parliament change any part of the Constitution? In 1973, the Supreme Court gave an answer that still holds.
Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368.
Kesavananda Bharati, head of a mutt in Kerala, went to court against state laws that took over the mutt's land. It grew into a much bigger question.
Thirteen judges heard it, the largest bench in the court's history. The hearing ran for sixty-eight days.
On the twenty-fourth of April, 1973, they decided, by seven votes to six.
Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution. But it cannot destroy its basic structure.
What counts as basic structure? Courts have named the supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, federalism and secularism, among others.
For Mains: name the case, cite Article 368, and explain basic structure in one line.

sources: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, (1973) 4 SCC 225, decided 24 April 1973; 13-judge bench, 7:6
Hearing of 68 days (31 Oct 1972 – 23 Mar 1973), per Supreme Court of India records and standard texts (M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity)
Basic structure elements named in later cases: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980), S.R. Bommai (1994)

quiz.q: Under which Article can Parliament amend the Constitution?
quiz.why: Article 368 gives Parliament the power to amend.
Thirteen judges, the largest bench ever, split seven to six.

options: Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights at all
Parliament can amend any part, but not destroy the basic structure
Only states can amend the Constitution
quiz.why: Any part may be amended, but the basic structure must stand.
